notes: Planning JR quashing Farnborough retail permissions; Simplex test and Martin v Wilson Homes construction applied.

enrichment.short_title: Legal & General v Rushmoor: quashing retail park permissions for misreading s.106 restriction
key_facts: Rushmoor granted Pillar planning permission to subdivide a former B&Q retail warehouse at Farnborough and erect additional units, relying on a section 106 agreement for site-wide controls.
The council and Pillar wrongly believed a 1993 planning obligation limiting use to durable goods applied only to the 1992 building, not the 1995 extension or garden centre land.
Neighbouring landowners challenged the permissions and the conditional section 106 deed as ultra vires.
Collins J quashed both permissions because the error was not trivial and a different outcome on conditions and section 106 benefits was reasonably possible.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of two planning permissions and a section 106 agreement at Farnborough.
enrichment.outcome: Both planning permissions were quashed; the section 106 obligation fell away with the second permission; the subdivision-only ground failed following Martin v David Wilson Homes.
enrichment.ratio: Where a planning authority materially misreads the extent of an existing section 106 restriction on durable-goods retail use, relief should not be withheld unless it is inevitable the same decision would have been made; under Simplex, an insubstantial error may justify discretion to uphold a decision, but a non-trivial misunderstanding of binding obligations requires quashing if a different package of conditions or benefits might have resulted.
legal_issues: Whether the 1993 obligation limited durable-goods use across the whole defined premises including the 1995 extension
Whether 'solely as a retail warehouse' prohibited subdivision into multiple units
Whether Mount Cook discretionary refusal principles applied to the claimants' motives
Whether quashing was necessary given Pillar's fallback position on subdivision and mezzanine floors

Simplex G.E. (Holdings) v Secretary of State for the Environment (1988) 57 P&CR 306
Martin v David Wilson Homes Ltd [2004] EWCA Civ 1027

notes: Interlocutory slander judgment on joinder, default judgment, s.32A and McManus republication principles.

enrichment.short_title: Sarayiah v Suren: joinder and limitation in media-industry slander action
key_facts: Mr Sarayiah sued over slanderous allegations of harassment and stalking made to police and his literary agency PFD, causing loss of a valuable representation contract.
Third, fourth and fifth defendants were joined without notice under CPR 19.5 after Master Hoffman dismissed joinder applications; Roderick Evans J allowed the appeal.
The third defendant obtained default judgment set aside; the new defendants applied under CPR 23.10 to vary the joinder order as time-barred.
Gray J had refused an interim injunction; the claimant was later convicted of harassing the first defendant, strengthening justification defences.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications to set aside default judgment, vary ex parte joinder, extend time, and for payment into court in a slander claim.
enrichment.outcome: Default judgment against the third defendant was set aside; joinder of the third to fifth defendants was varied and they were removed; section 32A discretion was refused; payment-into-court application dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Joinder under CPR 19.5 after expiry of the limitation period requires necessity, not mere desirability, for recovery or injunction purposes; ex parte joinder may be challenged under CPR 23.10; in defamation, section 32A relief turns on equitable balance including claim strength, delay and prejudice, and a separate harassment conviction may support justification under sections 5 and 13.
legal_issues: Whether joinder of time-barred defendants was necessary under CPR 19.5(3)
Whether the third defendant had a real prospect of defending republication under McManus v Beckham
Whether section 32A should disapply the one-year defamation limitation period
Whether qualified privilege and harassment conviction supported setting aside default judgment

Steedman v British Broadcasting Corporation [2001] EWCA Civ 1534

notes: Pharmaceutical settlement agreement; exclusive jurisdiction clause upheld and stay refused.

enrichment.short_title: DSM v GSK: stay refused where strain dispute falls within English exclusive jurisdiction clause
key_facts: DSM and GSK settled Dutch patent proceedings in 1997 by an English-law agreement barring GSK from objecting to DSM's use of the Annex VII Streptomyces strain.
GSK later alleged DSM was using stolen SC7 strain and commenced Pennsylvania proceedings against Teva, Ranbaxy and DSM.
DSM commenced English declaratory proceedings seeking relief that it used Annex VII strains, not SC7, and an anti-suit injunction.
Lewison J refused a forum non conveniens stay; the Court of Appeal dismissed GSK's appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of a stay of English proceedings under CPR Part 11 and case management powers.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the dispute whether DSM used SC7 or the Annex VII strain was held to be in connection with the settlement agreement and within the exclusive English jurisdiction clause.
enrichment.ratio: A dispute whether a party has used a permitted strain or misappropriated a rival strain is connected with a settlement agreement that bars objections to the permitted strain; clause 14 reserving US potassium clavulanate rights does not oust clause 15's exclusive English jurisdiction for that factual dispute, and a generous interpretation should be given to 'in connection with' jurisdiction clauses.
legal_issues: Construction of exclusive jurisdiction and USA exclusion clauses in the 1997 settlement
Whether the strain-identity dispute was connected with the agreement for clause 15 purposes
Whether Pennsylvania was a more appropriate forum
Whether Brussels Regulation Article 2 precluded a forum non conveniens stay

Owusu v Jackson [2003] PIQR 186
Travelers Casualty and Surety Company of Europe Ltd v Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada (UK) Ltd [2004] EWHC 1704

notes: Hague Convention summary return refused on children's objections; consent and acquiescence not proved.

enrichment.short_title: H v H: Hague Convention return refused where children objected to Australia
key_facts: An Australian father sought summary return of two children aged 11 and 9 after the mother retained them in England beyond an agreed three-to-four-month visit.
The mother argued consent, acquiescence and that the children objected to return under Article 13 of the Hague Convention.
Contemporaneous emails showed the father believed he had been deceived and sought legal advice on compelling return but was told he could not.
A CAFCASS officer found both children clearly objected to returning, citing settlement in England, friends, school and negative views of their father.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Hague Convention application for summary return of children wrongfully retained in England.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; consent and acquiescence were not proved but children's objections under Article 13 were established and discretion exercised against return.
enrichment.ratio: Article 13 children's objections require gateway findings that the child objects and has sufficient age and maturity; objections may encompass preference to remain where settled and fear of a parent, and where wrong legal advice explains delayed enforcement the subjective acquiescence defence may fail even if conduct appeared acquiescent.
legal_issues: Whether the father consented to permanent removal before June 2003
Whether he acquiesced after learning the mother would not return
Whether incorrect Australian legal advice negated acquiescence under Re: H
Whether children aged 9 and 11 had mature objections to return to Australia

notes: Youth court adjournment JR refused; CPS primary disclosure failure did not render decision irrational.

enrichment.short_title: W v Camberwell Youth Court: JR refused over robbery trial adjournment
key_facts: A 14-year-old faced robbery charges in the youth court after repeated failures to surrender to bail.
On the first trial date the Crown failed primary disclosure including an interview tape, and applied to adjourn to November.
Justices granted the adjournment but rightly refused an extension of custody time limits for lack of due diligence.
The defendant sought judicial review to quash the adjournment; the trial was later brought forward to September.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a youth court decision granting the prosecution an adjournment for disclosure failure.
enrichment.outcome: Claim refused; the adjournment was a lawful exercise of discretion despite sparse reasons and inexcusable CPS inefficiency.
enrichment.ratio: Decisions to grant or refuse adjournments in criminal proceedings are highly discretionary; courts will interfere only on clear grounds such as substantial unfairness, and failure to comply with disclosure obligations, while deserving rigorous scrutiny, does not automatically invalidate an adjournment where there is no defence prejudice and public interest favours trial of a serious offence.
legal_issues: Whether justices failed to consider relevant factors when granting the adjournment
Whether CPS disclosure failure required refusal of adjournment
Whether the defendant suffered prejudice from delay between July and September
Whether sparse reasons rendered the decision unlawful

notes: Leaving care pathway plan declaration; Newham failed Children Act and 2001 Regulations duties.

enrichment.short_title: P v Newham: declaration for missing leaving-care pathway plan for disabled child
key_facts: P, a severely disabled looked-after child approaching 18, had been placed in a children's centre after foster care broke down.
His grandmother complained that Newham had not produced the statutory needs assessment and pathway plan required for eligible children.
The authority had used an alternative transitional plan keeping P in placement until about 19, which did not comply with the statute.
Ouseley J declared non-compliance and ordered draft and final pathway plans by October 2004 with further review listed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of failure to assess needs and prepare a leaving-care pathway plan under the Children Act 1989 and 2001 Regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration that Newham failed its statutory duties; mandatory orders for assessment and pathway plan by specified dates; damages and HRA claims adjourned; costs to claimant.
enrichment.ratio: For an eligible looked-after child the local authority must carry out a statutory needs assessment and prepare a pathway plan under Schedule 2 paragraph 19B(4) and the Leaving Care Regulations; an internally preferred transitional process cannot substitute for compliance even where the child's immediate care needs are being met.
legal_issues: Whether Newham complied with Schedule 2 paragraph 19B(4) assessment and pathway plan duties
Whether an alternative transitional plan could lawfully replace the statutory framework
What timetable was appropriate given P's imminent 18th birthday
Whether Human Rights Act damages or further relief should be granted

confidence.notes: Statutory breach was conceded; declaration and remedial orders are explicit.

notes: SENDIST disability definition appeal; tribunal applied wrong severity test under DDA 1995.

enrichment.short_title: A v Hob Moor: SENDIST disability decision quashed for wrong DDA test
key_facts: Six-year-old A was withdrawn from primary school amid alleged disability discrimination over incontinence and global developmental delay.
SENDIST struck out the claim on the preliminary ground that A was not a disabled person under the DDA 1995.
The tribunal assessed severity of diagnosis and school functioning rather than whether impairments had a substantial adverse effect on normal day-to-day activities.
Supported by the Disability Rights Commission, the mother appealed; the school and tribunal did not oppose quashing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 against a SENDIST preliminary disability ruling.
enrichment.outcome: SENDIST decision quashed and remitted; tribunal had erred in applying a severity or diagnosis test instead of the statutory substantial adverse effect test.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 1 of the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 disability depends on whether a physical or mental impairment has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on normal day-to-day activities, not on whether a diagnosed condition is severe; continence and developmental delay must be assessed by that statutory test and relevant guidance, including the under-six deeming provision.
legal_issues: Whether A's incontinence and global developmental delay amounted to disability under section 1
Whether SENDIST wrongly required severe impairment or substantial difficulties in school skills
Application of Secretary of State guidance on continence and substantial effect
Effect of paragraph 6 deeming provision for children under six

notes: Asylum appeal dismissed; IAT entitled to prefer updated CIPU report on Eritrea return risk.

enrichment.short_title: SSHD v Haile: asylum appeal dismissed on objective country evidence
key_facts: An Eritrean minor claimed asylum based on low-level ELF opposition activity, detention, torture and escape after his activist father was killed.
An adjudicator allowed the appeal on asylum and human rights grounds; the Immigration Appeal Tribunal restored the refusal.
The IAT preferred the 2003 CIPU report showing returning ELF-RC members had not faced repercussions if they renounced opposition.
The Court of Appeal held the IAT was entitled to find no current well-founded fear despite credible past persecution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision restoring the Secretary of State's asylum refusal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no material error of law in the IAT's assessment of objective evidence on risk on return to Eritrea.
enrichment.ratio: On asylum appeals the tribunal may interfere with an adjudicator's view of objective country evidence where objective grounds require a different conclusion; membership of an exile ELF branch in the UK without activity attracting authority attention does not establish risk, and updated reliable country guidance may outweigh individual past detention where low-level activity is involved.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT erred in preferring the 2003 CIPU report over the adjudicator's findings
Whether past detention, torture and escape necessarily established current risk
Relevance of post-arrival ELF membership in London
Application of Subesh and Indrakumar standards of appellate review
linked_authorities: Subesh [2004] EWCA Civ 56
Indrakumar [2003] EWCA Civ 1677

notes: Judicial review of Leicester funding decisions; consultation failure clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: Leicester voluntary sector funding: consultation failure quashes decisions
key_facts: Service-user representatives challenged Leicester City Council decisions to cease funding six voluntary organisations.
Decision letters dated 25-26 February 2004 notified withdrawal of longstanding funding.
Claimants contended inadequate consultation and unequal treatment compared with council volunteers.
Council argued political policy change and disputed comparator point.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of funding cessation decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Six decision letters quashed for failure properly to consult; council may reconsult if it still wishes to change funding.
enrichment.ratio: Funding cessation decisions must comply with fair consultation (formative stage, adequate information, time, conscientious consideration); merits of political funding choices are not for the court; appraisal and reasons points need not be decided once consultation failure is established.
legal_issues: Fair consultation standards for local authority funding decisions
Whether comparator treatment of council volunteers was unlawful
Adequacy of reasons and appraisal process
Remedy when consultation defective

notes: Permission to appeal refused on mortgage possession; no appeal from second refusal under Access to Justice Act 1999.

enrichment.short_title: Moyse v Regal Mortgages: no further appeal from refused mortgage possession stay
key_facts: Regal Mortgages sought possession of Mr and Mrs Moyse's home for over £200,000 mortgage arrears unpaid for ten years.
The defendants argued a separate dispute with Guardian Assurance and an adviser Mr Verstage gave them a cross-claim that should stay possession.
District Judge White refused to suspend the warrant; Judge Cotterill refused permission to appeal twice, ending the county court route.
Grigson J's purported transfer to the Court of Appeal and suspension was declared a nullity by Cooke J; Brooke LJ refused permission to appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal after refusal of permission by a circuit judge in mortgage possession proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; no stay of eviction; Grigson J's order treated as a nullity; possession enforcement could proceed.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 54(4) of the Access to Justice Act 1999 there is no further appeal to the Court of Appeal once a circuit judge refuses permission to appeal on the papers and after an oral renewal; an ancillary stay pending a permission hearing falls away automatically and cannot itself be appealed, and possession will not be suspended where there is no prospect of paying current instalments and any related financial mis-selling claim is separate from the assignee mortgagee's enforcement rights.
legal_issues: Whether any appeal lay against Judge Cotterill's refusal of permission and removal of stay
Whether Grigson J had jurisdiction to transfer a non-existent appeal to the Court of Appeal
Whether separate regulatory or mis-selling claims justified suspending possession
Whether assignee Regal Mortgages could enforce regardless of Guardian Assurance liability
